Ḍāmara Tantra
------------------------------------------
In the डामर class of तन्त्रस्, शिव as Unmatta भैरव teaches पार्वती as Unmatta भैरवी who starts the work with various questions.
The work mentions 8 Unmatta Bhairavas like Kapāli भैरव, सṁहार भैरव and Krodha भैरव.
It has six paricchedas or chapters plus a chapter called Maṅgalācaraṇa. The whole work is in the śloka (anuṣṭubh) metre, except for the mantras which are in prose.
It is a work of the वामाचार tantra group dealing with what is called ‘Ṣaṭkarmas’. They are: stambhana (arresting all movement); mohana (creating delusions); उच्चाटन (driving away); vidveṣaṇa (creating enmity); vaśīkaraṇa (enslaving); māraṇa (killing).
Under each of the षट्कर्मस्, many details are given.
For instance:
Under vaśīkaraṇa: how to control the king, a wicked woman, one’s own husband.
Under stambhana: how to stop a ship, a fire, an enemy.
Under māraṇa: how to kill the horse of the enemy, to destroy the clothes of a washerman, to destroy the milk of the milk-vendor and so on.
The various mantras to be used in such acts, as also the rites connected with them, are also given.
However, no one should attempt them without valid reasons acceptable to धर्म. And, they can be done only under expert guidance.

ḍamaru
(‘a small drum’)
------------------------------------------
Pictures and images of शिव (one of the major forms of God in हिन्दुइस्म्) show him as holding the त्रिशूल (trident) and the डमरु (a small drum) in his hands.
The डमरु which is a folk or tribal musical instrument of the percussion type, is in extensive use even now in the rural parts of India, especially by the folk-dancers and priests of the tāntrik tradition. It is a sort of kettle-drum, very small in size. It is made of two inverted bowls of wood or clay, the open ends being covered with parchment or thin leather. Strings with beads at their ends are attached to the slender middle portion. When the drum is rhythmically shaken by hand, a pleasant rattling sound is produced, as the beads strike the membrane on the open ends.
In the images of शिव (especially the dancing ones like नटराज) the डमरु is held in the upper right hand.
According to some mythological accounts, शिव, at the request of the gods in हेअवेन्, is said to have danced with power and grace—a rare combination indeed—using the डमरु and sounding it fourteen times. Each time, the sound that emerged, formed a specific pattern, giving rise to the fourteen basic aphorisms of Sanskrit grammar (called Māheśvara-sūtras, like ‘a-i-uṇ,’ ‘ṛ-lṛk’ and so on). Consequently the symbolical meaning of the डमरु in शिव’s hand is sound or alphabets or grammar or language. It may also represent the आकाश or the ether principle, the first of the five basic elements in the process of च्रेअतिओन् of the world.
See also ŚIVA.
